Hello revivalfx, it looks like you're fairly new here so welcome to RTM.

I think what's meant by CPLQ is: compression that leads to heavy liquidity of one type. For instance, price compresses up to a supply zone where sell orders far exceed buy orders - compression leading to sell-side liquidity.

As for your #1 and #2, I think both are correct. Sure, compression eats liquidity from both sides, but in the tight range both buys and sells are fairly evenly matched, and in the above example, price cannot make a parabolic move downward until sells absolutely overtake buys. Compression gets price to that absolute, even if that means the compression enters the zone we've drawn or moves through the zone to a higher supply zone with more sells waiting.

As for the formation, I wouldn't presume to speak for anyone on this site, but it seems like the most experienced among us pay less attention to the look of an individual candle(s) and more to the zones they create, and more specifically the orders behind the zones they create. Does a pinbar matter because of its shape after-the-fact or because demand exceed supply to drive price up where it found supply and dropped back near where price opened that bar's timeframe? In other words, the orders that created the zone that ultimately translated into a pinbar is what's important, not the bar's look/name afterwards. Where the zone occurs is also hugely important, as is who is creating the zone to begin with. These ideas have been (and continue to be) huge learning points for me - what is the smart money trying to hide from everyone else in this zone on the chart? In compression they are removing orders to make it easier to move price through that area of the chart in the future.

As you said in your P.S., if my comments above don't help you process things, it could very well be that I need to study it more. I think a lot of this has been said better elsewhere including these thoughts and charts from some of the experts: readthemarket.com/index.php/forum/journa...-on-course?start=143

Hi anneb5,

I think you might be seeing the play backwards. On my chart, you would enter at the demand I'd marked up - entering long to the top of the compression zone. On your chart, while for the most part I agree with how you've highlighted things, there are a few things I'd change from my experience. The first one is that the "H1 Supply" at the top of the compression zone may act like supply but I don't consider it to be supply myself. If you notice, it was spiked just as the other areas were in the compression zone so it should have those orders filled already. What it is, however, is often a take profit area which sometimes starts a selloff. The blue H1 Demand right below the consumed demand zones is an area I'd probably define a little more broadly. See my graphic for where I put the top/proximal line for that demand zone. Now if you were to have missed it because of being more conservative on zones, that's okay too - a friend of mine has a saying, that trades are like a bus. There's always another one coming around the corner!

Thanks Kanzler.. these are details I do wonder about. I noticed after I had posted, that your proximal line was further out. And I see that that is probably where price has more definitely been taken out by the buyers. This sometimes looks different on a different TF too. Looking at my chart again, probably the demand zone below that one should also be wider. Nice point about spiked supply being a take profit area. I hadn't thought of it like that -that helps. I think I need to do a fair bit more study before I take too many buses! It seems that the ankle bone is connected to the knee bone etc and it possibly won't be until I've made my way through all chapters that it hangs together a bit more completely. Cheers.

No problem. The whole issue of proximal/distal lines on the supply/demand is going to be up to you. Sometimes I draw them farther out, sometimes closer depending on the situation. For example I might be really liberal on widening the zone in the case of targeting a supply/demand zone since I don't want to compete for an exit and miss my chance to take profit. It's not an exact science either, I'm still learning a lot myself.
This is probably not Compression anymore.. but defining the s and d zones is pretty important...
